claim: The outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria contains lipopolysaccharides (LPS) and phospholipids (PLs) in the outer and inner leaflets, respectively.
source: Unlike the inner membrane (IM), which is a phospholipid (PL) bilayer, the OM contains lipopolysaccharides (LPS) and PLs in the outer and inner leaflets, respectively (Kamio and Nikaido, 1976).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kamio and Nikaido, 1976.

claim: Lipid asymmetry in the outer membrane renders it impermeable to a wide range of compounds, including hydrophobic molecules.
source: This unique lipid asymmetry, characterized by a tightly-packed LPS outer leaflet, renders the OM impermeable to a wide range of compounds, including hydrophobic molecules (Nikaido, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nikaido, 2003.

claim: During growth or stress, phospholipids may appear in the outer leaflet of the outer membrane.
source: During growth or in the event of stress, PLs may appear in the outer leaflet of the OM (Jia et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2006; Dalebroux et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jia et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2006; Dalebroux et al., 2014.

claim: OmpLA cleaves both acyl chains from the glycerol backbone of phospholipids.
source: OmpLA cleaves both acyl chains from the glycerol backbone of PLs (Dekker, 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dekker, 2000.

claim: PagP transfers one acyl chain from phospholipids to LPS or phosphatidylglycerol (PG).
source: PagP transfers one acyl chain from PLs to LPS (Bishop, 2005) or phosphatidylglycerol (PG) (Dalebroux et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bishop, 2005 and Dalebroux et al., 2014.

claim: The OmpC-Mla system maintains outer membrane lipid asymmetry by removing phospholipids from the outer membrane and transporting them back to the inner membrane.
source: In addition, the OmpC-Mla system is thought to maintain OM lipid asymmetry by removing PLs from the OM and transporting them back to the IM (Malinverni and Silhavy, 2009; Chong et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Malinverni and Silhavy, 2009; Chong et al., 2015.

claim: MlaE and MlaF are predicted to form the transmembrane domains (TMDs) and nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs) of an ABC transporter, respectively.
source: MlaE and MlaF constitute the core components of the ABC transporter and are predicted to form the transmembrane domains (TMDs) and nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs), respectively (Malinverni and Silhavy, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Malinverni and Silhavy, 2009.

claim: MlaD, MlaE, and MlaF are conserved across many species of Gram-negative bacteria and can also be found in actinomycetes and plants.
source: Consistent with this idea, MlaD, along with MlaE and MlaF, are conserved across many species of Gram-negative bacteria and can also be found in actinomycetes (Casali and Riley, 2007) and in plants (Benning, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Casali and Riley, 2007 and Benning, 2009.

claim: The Mce4 pathway in Mycobacterium tuberculosis is important for cholesterol uptake.
source: The Mce4 pathway in Mycobacterium tuberculosis is important for cholesterol uptake (Pandey and Sassetti, 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pandey and Sassetti, 2008.

claim: The TGD system in the chloroplasts of Arabidopsis thaliana functions to transport phosphatidic acid (PA) from the plastid outer membrane to the inner membrane.
source: the TGD system in the chloroplasts of Arabidopsis thaliana functions to transport phosphatidic acid (PA) from the plastid OM to the IM (Benning, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Benning, 2009.

claim: MlaB contains a STAS domain that is believed to have a general nucleoside triphosphate (NTP) binding function.
source: MlaB contains a Sulfate Transporter and Anti-Sigma factor antagonist (STAS) domain that is believed to have a general nucleoside triphosphate (NTP) binding function (Aravind and Koonin, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aravind and Koonin, 2000.

claim: MlaF, MlaE, MlaD and MlaB interact specifically with each other to form a stable complex.
source: We show that MlaF, MlaE, MlaD and MlaB interact specifically with each other to form a stable complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by affinity purification experiments and SEC analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: His-MlaE is functional and can restore SDS/EDTA resistance in the ΔmlaE mutant strain.
source: This construct is fully functional, as it is able to restore SDS/EDTA resistance in the ΔmlaE mutant strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MlaF and MlaD co-purify with His-MlaE.
source: Two unique protein bands at ~29 kDa and ~19 kDa co-purified with His-MlaE (Figure 1A). These bands represent MlaF and MlaD, respectively, as they are no longer co-purified in the corresponding ΔmlaF and ΔmlaD mutant strains.
evidence: The claim is supported by affinity purification data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: His-MlaE migrates anomalously as a diffuse band around 24 kDa when samples are not heated.
source: His-MlaE migrates anomalously as a diffuse band around 24 kDa (expected 28 kDa), likely because it is still partially folded in the presence of SDS, a phenomenon commonly observed for multi-pass membrane proteins (Rath et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1A and a citation to Rath et al., 2009.

claim: MlaD migrates as a high molecular weight species when samples are not heated, suggesting oligomer formation.
source: Remarkably, MlaD also migrates differently, now as a high molecular weight species, when the samples are not heated, suggesting that it may be forming oligomers.
evidence: The claim is supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: MlaF-His and MlaD-His are functional.
source: we performed reciprocal affinity purification experiments using WT cells expressing C-terminally His-tagged MlaF (MlaF-His) or MlaD (MlaD-His) proteins, which we show are functional (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MlaF-His and MlaD-His can pull down MlaD and MlaF, respectively.
source: we demonstrate that MlaF-His and MlaD-His are able to pull down MlaD and MlaF, respectively, likely via interactions with MlaE (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by affinity purification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: MlaC does not co-purify with the MlaFEDB complex.
source: Even though we also expressed MlaC, it was not co-purified with the rest of the complex.
evidence: The claim is based on purification experiments described in the text.

claim: Interactions between MlaC and the inner membrane complex may be weak and/or transient.
source: This suggests that interactions between MlaC and the IM complex may be weak and/or transient, in line with the idea that it is a periplasmic binding protein (Malinverni and Silhavy, 2009).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that MlaC does not co-purify with the complex, supported by a citation to Malinverni and Silhavy, 2009.

claim: The soluble domain of MlaD (sMlaD-His) forms hexamers.
source: Multi-angle light scattering (MALS) analysis revealed that the absolute molar mass of purified sMlaD-His is ~110.7 kDa, establishing that these are in fact hexamers (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The experimental molar mass of the MlaFEDB complex is consistent with the presence of six copies of MlaD.
source: Furthermore, the experimental molar mass of the MlaFEDB complex (~285 kDa by SEC-MALS) is consistent with the presence of six copies of MlaD (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Hexamers formed by sMlaD-His alone are resistant to SDS denaturation.
source: Remarkably, hexamers formed by sMlaD-His alone are also resistant to SDS denaturation (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Oligomerization and extreme stability are unique properties of the soluble domain of MlaD.
source: These results indicate that oligomerization and extreme stability are unique properties of the soluble domain.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that the soluble domain alone forms stable hexamers.

claim: TGD2 in Arabidopsis thaliana is the direct homolog of MlaD and was found to bind phosphatidic acid (PA).
source: In this system, TGD2 is the direct homolog of MlaD and was found to bind PA (Awai et al., 2006; Roston et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Awai et al., 2006; Roston et al., 2011.

claim: Purified sMlaD-His contains bound phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and phosphatidylglycerol (PG).
source: We detected both phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and PG bound to sMlaD-His (Figure 3A and B) but not to dLolB-His (Figure 3A), indicating that MlaD has affinity for PLs.
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC and 31P NMR data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Delipidated LolB (dLolB-His) does not bind phospholipids.
source: We detected both phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and PG bound to sMlaD-His (Figure 3A and B) but not to dLolB-His (Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Comparable amounts of PE and PG (~1:1) co-purified with sMlaD-His despite PE being the predominant lipid in E. coli cellular extracts.
source: Comparable amounts of PE and PG (~1:1) co-purified with sMlaD-His despite PE being the predominant lipid in E. coli cellular extracts (~72% PE, 17% PG, 11% cardiolipin (CL)) (Lugtenberg and Peters, 1976) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by 31P NMR data shown in Figure 3B and a citation to Lugtenberg and Peters, 1976.

claim: MlaD may have a preference for binding PG.
source: These results suggest that MlaD may have a preference for binding PG.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that equal amounts of PE and PG co-purify with MlaD despite PE being more abundant in cells.

claim: Native mass spectrometry indicates the presence of at least four bound phospholipid molecules in hexameric sMlaD-His.
source: Deconvolution of the native MS spectrum indicates the molecular weight of the native hexamers to be ~110 kDa, suggesting the presence of at least four bound PL molecules (~750 Da each, in agreement with the average mass of PE and PG) and therefore, strong protein-PL interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by native MS data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The presence of ligands is not strictly required for the formation of sMlaD hexamers.
source: By increasing the collision energy in the mass spectrometer collision cell, we are then able to destabilize the native structure, revealing the presence of hexamers binding three, two, one or zero PL molecules (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B). This suggests that the presence of ligands is not strictly required for the formation of sMlaD hexamers.
evidence: The claim is supported by native MS data with increasing collision energies shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Hexameric sMlaD is a phospholipid-binding complex with at least four binding sites.
source: Taken together, our data establish that hexameric sMlaD is a PL-binding complex with at least four binding sites.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the data from TLC, NMR, and native MS experiments.

claim: MlaB is required for the assembly of the MlaFE complex.
source: Therefore, MlaF does not interact with MlaE unless MlaB is present.
evidence: The claim is supported by purification experiments showing that MlaF does not co-purify with His-MlaE in the absence of MlaB (Figure 4A, B, D).

claim: MlaF is not co-purified with His-MlaE in preparations of MlaFE and MlaFED.
source: Despite reasonable expression of MlaF (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), it is not co-purified with His-MlaE in preparations of MlaFE and MlaFED (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEC and SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: MlaF is not co-purified with His-MlaE in the absence of MlaB in cells expressing His-MlaE at low levels.
source: Unlike in WT cells, MlaF is not co-purified with His-MlaE in the absence of MlaB (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by affinity purification data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: MlaF-His could not pull down MlaD without MlaB.
source: Similarly, we show that MlaF-His could not pull down MlaD (through MlaE) without MlaB (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by affinity purification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The affinity-enriched levels of MlaF-His appear to be reduced in the absence of MlaB, suggesting that MlaB modulates the stability of MlaF.
source: In fact, the affinity-enriched levels of MlaF-His appear to be reduced in the absence of MlaB, suggesting that MlaB modulates the stability of MlaF.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that less MlaF-His is recovered in the absence of MlaB.

claim: MlaB plays a key role in the assembly of the MlaFEDB complex.
source: Our results demonstrate that MlaB plays a key role in the assembly of the complex.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the data showing that MlaB is required for complex assembly.

claim: The T52A mutation in MlaB does not affect the assembly of the MlaFEB complex.
source: This mutation does not affect the assembly of the MlaFEB complex (Figure 5A)
evidence: The claim is supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: MlaFEBWT exhibits high intrinsic ATPase activity in detergent micelles with kcat = 1.8 ± 0.5 μmol ATP s-1/μmol complex.
source: We demonstrate that MlaFEBWT exhibits high intrinsic ATPase activity in detergent micelles (kcat = 1.8 ± 0.5 μmol ATP s-1/μmol complex) (Figure 5A)
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme-coupled ATPase assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ATP binding is cooperative in MlaFEBWT with a Hill coefficient = 1.5 ± 0.5.
source: In addition, ATP binding is cooperative (Hill coefficient = 1.5 ± 0.5).
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme-coupled ATPase assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No ATPase activity is detected with the MlaFEBT52A complex.
source: Remarkably, no activity is detected with the MlaFEBT52A complex, similar to a variant of the complex containing a predicted non-functional mutation in the MlaF Walker A motif (MlaFK47REB) (Walker et al., 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme-coupled ATPase assay data shown in Figure 5A and a citation to Walker et al., 1982.

claim: The mlaBT52A allele does not complement SDS-EDTA sensitivity observed in ΔmlaB strains.
source: Accordingly, the mlaBT52A or mlaFK47R alleles do not complement SDS-EDTA sensitivity observed in ΔmlaB and ΔmlaF strains, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by OM permeability assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mlaFK47R allele does not complement SDS-EDTA sensitivity observed in ΔmlaF strains.
source: Accordingly, the mlaBT52A or mlaFK47R alleles do not complement SDS-EDTA sensitivity observed in ΔmlaB and ΔmlaF strains, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by OM permeability assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: MlaB assumes critical role(s) during catalysis.
source: These results imply that MlaB assumes critical role(s) during catalysis
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that the T52A mutation abolishes ATPase activity.

claim: The presence of MlaD in the MlaFEDB complex does not significantly affect the affinity of the complex for ATP.
source: We show that the association of MlaD with MlaFEB does not significantly affect the affinity of the complex for ATP (Km = 181.1 ± 203.6 μM for MlaFEDB vs 161.4 ± 75.57 μM for MlaFEB) (Figure 5A)
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme-coupled ATPase assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The presence of MlaD in the MlaFEDB complex reduces ATP hydrolytic activity by ~3-fold.
source: however, its presence in the MlaFEDB complex reduces ATP hydrolytic activity by ~3-fold (kcat = 0.6 ± 0.3 μmol ATP s-1/μmol complex)
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme-coupled ATPase assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The presence of MlaD affects cooperativity of ATP binding with a Hill coefficient = 1.0 ± 0.6 for MlaFEDB.
source: and affects cooperativity (Hill coefficient = 1.0 ± 0.6).
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme-coupled ATPase assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: MlaD interacts with the ABC transporter solely via MlaE.
source: Given that the MlaED complex can be stably isolated (Figures 1A and 4B), and that MlaD does not co-purify with MlaF-His in the absence of MlaE (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), it is likely that MlaD interacts with the ABC transporter solely via MlaE.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on purification data shown in Figures 1A, 4B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Interaction between MlaD and MlaE may cause structural changes in MlaF and/or directly influence how the two NBDs come together to perform catalysis.
source: Our findings suggest that such an interaction may cause structural changes in MlaF (the NBDs) and/or directly influence how the two NBDs come together to perform catalysis.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the observation that MlaD affects ATPase activity.

claim: MlaD forms SDS-resistant hexamers within the MlaFEDB complex.
source: Within this complex, we have demonstrated that MlaD forms SDS-resistant hexamers
evidence: The claim is supported by SDS-PAGE and SEC-MALS data shown in Figures 1B and 2.

claim: MlaD co-purifies with phospholipids.
source: and co-purifies with PLs.
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC, NMR, and native MS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: MlaD modulates the ATPase activity of the complex via its interaction with MlaE.
source: We have also revealed that MlaD modulates the ATPase activity of the complex via its interaction with MlaE.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: MlaB plays critical roles in both the assembly and activity of the ABC transporter.
source: Finally, we have established multiple roles for MlaB in both the assembly and activity of the ABC transporter
evidence: The claim is supported by purification and ATPase assay data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: A single T52A mutation in MlaB separates its assembly and activity functions.
source: and have identified a single mutation in MlaB that separated these two functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that the T52A mutation does not affect assembly but abolishes activity (Figure 5A).

claim: ATP hydrolytic activity of some ABC transporters is intrinsically low and can only be activated upon the binding of the corresponding substrate-binding proteins.
source: For a few well-characterized transporters, ATP hydrolytic activity is intrinsically low and can only be activated upon the binding of the corresponding SBPs (Chen et al., 2001; Liu et al., 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2001; Liu et al., 1997.

claim: MlaFEB possesses high intrinsic ATPase activity that is attenuated by MlaD association.
source: we have demonstrated that MlaFEB possesses high intrinsic ATPase activity that is attenuated by MlaD association (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Interactions with MlaD may stabilize conformations that are inactive in ATP hydrolysis.
source: Interactions with MlaD may stabilize conformations that are inactive in ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the observation that MlaD reduces ATPase activity.

claim: MlaD may not have phospholipids bound in MlaFEDB preparations solubilized in detergent micelles.
source: Furthermore, because our MlaFEDB preparations are solubilized in detergent micelles, which can disrupt lipid binding, it may be possible that MlaD does not have PLs bound.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the state of MlaD in the purified complex.

claim: The complex may be unstimulated without bound substrates, resulting in low ATPase activity.
source: While this idea remains to be tested, the complex may be unstimulated without bound substrates, resulting in low ATPase activity (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is speculation about the mechanism of activity regulation.

claim: MlaD ensures that the full complex conserves ATP and retains the capacity to be activated only when MlaC binds and/or delivers the phospholipid substrate.
source: Our results suggest a function for MlaD in ensuring that the full complex conserves ATP, and presumably retains the capacity to be activated only when MlaC binds and/or delivers the PL substrate.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the observation that MlaD reduces ATPase activity.

claim: The MlaC homolog from Ralstonia solenacerum can be purified and crystallized as a soluble complex with PE.
source: However, the facts that the MlaC homolog from Ralstonia solenacerum can be purified and crystallized as a soluble complex with PE (Protein Data Bank ID: 2QGU; DOI: 10.2210/pdb2qgu/pdb)
evidence: The claim is supported by a reference to a Protein Data Bank entry.

claim: Strong interactions between MlaC and the OmpC-MlaA or MlaFEDB complexes were not detected.
source: and that we could not detect strong interactions between MlaC and the OmpC-MlaA (Chong et al., 2015) or MlaFEDB complexes
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and a citation to Chong et al., 2015.

claim: Mla-mediated phospholipid transport across the periplasm may proceed via a soluble intermediate.
source: indicate that Mla-mediated PL transport across the periplasm may proceed instead via a soluble intermediate.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the lack of strong interactions between MlaC and the complexes.

claim: Phospholipid transfer from the OmpC-MlaA complex to MlaC, and then to MlaD in the inner membrane complex, is largely driven by affinity.
source: In this alternative scenario, we posit that PL transfer from the OmpC-MlaA complex to MlaC, and then to MlaD in the IM complex, is largely driven by affinity (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is speculation about the mechanism of PL transfer.

claim: At least four of the six phospholipid binding sites in MlaD have reasonably high affinity for phospholipids.
source: At least four of these binding sites have reasonably high affinity for PLs, thereby facilitating co-purification with MlaD and detection in native MS analysis (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on native MS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: MlaD may have higher affinity for phospholipid substrates than MlaC, driving overall phospholipid transfer.
source: MlaD may have higher affinity for PL substrates than MlaC, driving overall PL transfer (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is speculation about the mechanism of PL transfer.

claim: The energy derived from ATP hydrolysis may be utilized to release bound phospholipids into the membrane by inducing conformational changes that alter phospholipid binding affinities within the MlaD oligomer.
source: In the MlaFEDB complex, the energy derived from ATP hydrolysis may then be utilized to release bound PLs into the membrane, perhaps by inducing conformational changes that alter PL binding affinities within the MlaD oligomer.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the mechanism of PL release.

claim: The hexameric architecture of MlaD, which contains the MCE domain, is conserved in homologs of the Mla system found in plants and actinomycetes.
source: We believe that the hexameric architecture of MlaD, which contains the MCE domain (Figure 2A), is conserved in homologs of the Mla system found in plants and actinomycetes.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the observation that MlaD forms hexamers and knowledge of homologous systems.

claim: TGD2 in Arabidopsis thaliana has been proposed to exist as an oligomer.
source: Here, the MlaD-like protein, TGD2, has been proposed to exist as an oligomer (Roston et al., 2011, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Roston et al., 2011, 2012.

claim: In Mycobacterium tuberculosis, there are four Mce systems, of which Mce4 is essential for cholesterol uptake and catabolism.
source: In M. tuberculosis, there are four Mce systems, of which Mce4 is essential for cholesterol uptake and catabolism (Pandey and Sassetti, 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pandey and Sassetti, 2008.

claim: Other Mce systems in Mycobacterium tuberculosis may have functions in transporting other lipids.
source: while others may have functions in transporting other lipids (Forrellad et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Forrellad et al., 2014.

claim: Mce operons in Mycobacterium tuberculosis comprise genes encoding two MlaE-like permeases and six MlaD-like (MCE) proteins.
source: These systems are expressed from operons each comprising genes encoding two MlaE-like permeases and six MlaD-like (MCE) proteins (Casali and Riley, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Casali and Riley, 2007.

claim: The organization of Mce operons suggests the assembly of ABC transporters containing a hetero-hexameric arrangement of MCE domains.
source: The organization of these operons suggests the assembly of ABC transporters containing a hetero-hexameric arrangement of MCE domains.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the organization of Mce operons.

claim: The hexameric MCE structure may be a general architecture for binding and transporting various lipid substrates.
source: This hexameric MCE structure may thus be a general architecture for binding and transporting various lipid substrates.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the observation that MlaD forms hexamers and knowledge of homologous systems.

claim: MlaD appears to be specific for PG over PE, the major phospholipids in E. coli.
source: MlaD appears to be specific for PG over PE, the major PLs in E. coli (Figure 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC and NMR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The observed preference for PG may reflect a higher affinity of MlaD for this lipid during purification conditions.
source: The observed preference for PG may reflect a higher affinity of MlaD for this lipid simply during purification conditions.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the reason for PG preference.

claim: The observed preference for PG may indicate specificity for PG during phospholipid transport.
source: Alternatively, it may indicate specificity for PG during PL transport.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the reason for PG preference.

claim: PG has a higher tendency to appear on the cell surface during normal growth, or removal of outer leaflet PG is more important to ensure outer membrane stability.
source: this finding suggests that either PG has a higher tendency to appear on the cell surface during normal growth, or removal of outer leaflet PG is more important to ensure OM stability.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the observation that MlaD preferentially binds PG.

claim: The outer membrane enzyme PagP has been evolved to acylate outer leaflet PG (in addition to LPS), but not PE, as a mechanism to fortify the outer membrane barrier.
source: Consistent with these ideas, the OM enzyme PagP has been evolved to acylate outer leaflet PG (in addition to LPS), but not PE, as a mechanism to fortify the OM barrier (Dalebroux et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dalebroux et al., 2014.

claim: The outer membrane has lower PG content than the inner membrane in E. coli and Salmonella Typhimurium.
source: It has also been reported that the OM has lower PG content than the IM in E. coli (Lugtenberg and Peters, 1976) and Salmonella Typhimurium (Osborn et al., 1972).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lugtenberg and Peters, 1976 and Osborn et al., 1972.

claim: An active PG-specific retrograde transport system could have utility in establishing the apparent differences in membrane phospholipid compositions.
source: While these observations are still controversial, an active PG-specific retrograde transport system could have utility in establishing the apparent differences in membrane PL compositions.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the function of the OmpC-Mla system.

claim: In the absence of MlaB, the canonical ABC transporter complex (MlaFE) could not be isolated owing to the decreased stability of MlaF and/or weakened interactions between MlaE and MlaF.
source: In the absence of MlaB, the canonical ABC transporter complex (MlaFE) could not be isolated (Figure 4A), owing to the decreased stability of MlaF and/or weakened interactions between MlaE and MlaF.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on purification data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A single T52A mutation in the STAS domain protein does not affect complex assembly but abolishes ATPase activity.
source: We have also established a separate role for MlaB in the activity of the complex; a single T52A mutation in the STAS domain protein does not affect complex assembly but abolishes ATPase activity (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by purification and ATPase assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: STAS domains have been reported to be critical for the assembly and activity of non-ABC family transporters, including the Sultr1;2 sulfate transporter in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: Corroborating these conclusions, we note that STAS domains have similarly been reported to be critical for the assembly and activity of non-ABC family transporters, including the Sultr1;2 sulfate transporter in A. thaliana (Shibagaki and Grossman, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shibagaki and Grossman, 2006.

claim: MlaB-like and MlaE-like domains can be found in the same polypeptides in some organisms.
source: In fact, MlaB-like and MlaE-like domains can be found in the same polypeptides in some organisms (Pfam accession number: PF13466) (Finn et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Finn et al., 2016.

claim: The T52A mutation removes a conserved threonine residue in MlaB that is mapped to a serine in the STAS domain anti-sigma factor antagonist, SpoIIAA, in Bacillus subtilis.
source: The T52A mutation removes a conserved threonine residue in MlaB that is mapped to a serine in the STAS domain anti-sigma factor antagonist, SpoIIAA, in Bacillus subtilis (Aravind and Koonin, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aravind and Koonin, 2000.

claim: The conserved serine in SpoIIAA can be phosphorylated by its target anti-sigma factor SpoIIAB, which disrupts the ability of SpoIIAA to bind SpoIIAB, presumably due to a conformational change.
source: This residue can be phosphorylated by its target anti-sigma factor SpoIIAB, which disrupts the ability of SpoIIAA to bind SpoIIAB, presumably due to a conformational change (Diederich et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Diederich et al., 1994.

claim: MlaB may become phosphorylated in cells.
source: By analogy, we hypothesize that MlaB may become phosphorylated in cells.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on analogy to SpoIIAA.

claim: Conformational changes associated with putative phosphorylation of MlaB might indirectly regulate MlaF and affect its function in ATP hydrolysis.
